content.thinking: I need to make sure I'm citing only record labels, not candidate names, and avoiding bare digits — using references like {T21.2} and {T21.3} instead of numbers, and {began}/{recovered} for timing. The flapping evidence seems to live only in one candidate's confirmed account, so I should ground my citations in the actual record entries covering replicas, the floor change, and related events rather than the candidate's framing.

action_items.item: Review the autoscaler's scale-down behaviour for io-shop, such as stabilization window and thresholds, so that capacity does not drop below what the current load uses. Add a load test with a traffic step to check it.
Decide whether the raised autoscaler floor on io-shop should stay. Then either make it permanent, with the sizing rationale recorded, or schedule its removal once the autoscaler fix is merged.
Add an alert on repeated changes in the autoscaler's capacity, and on CPU use at the limit, so that flapping is caught before it causes user-visible errors.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages and failures. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} for {duration}, and the logs show account page requests failing because shoppers closed the connection.

Requests were slow and shoppers gave up because the service did not have enough capacity at that moment. The metrics read back by the Investigator Agent show latency spikes at the times capacity was at its lower value.
Capacity was too low because the autoscaler held io-shop at a minimum of {T21.2} replicas and kept adding and reclaiming capacity instead of settling at the level the traffic needed.
No deploy, release or flag change preceded the incident, so it was not a release. The cause lies in how the autoscaler responded to the traffic.

Raising the autoscaler floor from {T21.2} to {T21.3} replicas stopped capacity from falling short, and the service was back at its baseline from the minute after the action. This supports the autoscaler as the cause.

contributing_factors.factor: The autoscaler configuration let capacity fall below what the load needed and did not settle. The underlying fix is still only a draft pull request.
The mitigation is a raised floor set by hand and still in place. Nothing records when it should be reviewed, and it may leave the service over-provisioned.

Nothing warned of the capacity flapping before shoppers were affected. The account page warnings in the logs were already firing in the minutes before the page, and the page came only at {alert_raised}.

input.executive_summary: The shop service io-shop had a brief spell of slow and failing requests, lasting {duration}. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken}. Shoppers on account pages were affected. No deploy or flag change preceded it. The automatic capacity controller kept adding and then removing capacity, so at times the service had too little. The response agent raised the minimum capacity, the metrics returned to baseline, and a draft code fix was proposed for review.

got_lucky: The impact was short and the error rate peaked at only {errors_at_worst}.
The higher floor was enough to absorb the traffic. Further growth could have outrun it.
went_well: The Investigator Agent read metrics, changes and logs and ranked the autoscaler explanation first. The Mitigation Agent confirmed the action worked.
Raising the autoscaler floor brought the service back to baseline, and the paging rule stopped firing.
A draft fix was proposed shortly after mitigation.
went_wrong: Warnings about the account page error rate appeared in the logs before the alert and nothing acted on them.
Capacity flapping was not detected by any alert of its own.

input.root_cause: The autoscaler for io-shop did not hold enough capacity. Its minimum was {T21.2} replicas, and capacity kept dropping back to a level the load had already outgrown, so latency rose and requests failed. Raising the floor to {T21.3} replicas held capacity steady and the service recovered.
input.symptom: Shop requests slowed and some failed
